lesson_scope: Trapezoidal journey modeling across three phases: acceleration, constant-speed cruising, and deceleration; algebraic formulation with deceleration-to-acceleration ratios, total journey constraints, quadratic velocity solutions, truncated trapezium models, and triangular speed optimizations under track speed limits.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Deceleration duration when deceleration rate is twice acceleration rate

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Deceleration duration when deceleration rate is twice acceleration rate

hints: The top speed reached is $V = aT$.
Deceleration rate is $2a$, so deceleration time is $\frac{V}{2a} = \frac{aT}{2a} = 0.5T$.

walkthrough.text:
Express the maximum speed $V$ in terms of acceleration $a$ and time $T$:
$$V = aT$$

Calculate the deceleration time using the deceleration magnitude $2a$:
$$t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{V}{2a} = \frac{aT}{2a} = 0.5T$$\text{The train takes } 0.5T\text{ seconds to decelerate to rest.}

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Relate speeds:
- Reached velocity:
$$V = aT$$

Divide by braking rate:
- Deceleration duration:
$$t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{aT}{2a} = 0.5T$$
Braking takes half as long as acceleration because deceleration is twice as large.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $t = \frac{V}{d}$ with $V = aT$ and $d = 2a$.
Simplifies to obtain $t_{\text{dec}} = 0.5T$ or $\frac{T}{2}$.

$$t_{\text{non-cruise}} = T + 0.5T = 1.5T$$

$$t_{\text{cruise}} = 120 - 1.5T$$\text{The cruising duration is } 120 - 1.5T\text{ seconds.}

- Acceleration plus braking:
$$t_{\text{acc}} + t_{\text{dec}} = T + 0.5T = 1.5T$$

Subtract from overall duration:
- Cruising interval:
$$t_{\text{cruise}} = 120 - 1.5T$$
The train cruises for $120 - 1.5T$ seconds.

hints: From $v^2 = 2as$, stopping distance is $s = \frac{V^2}{2d}$.

walkthrough.text:
Express the peak velocity in terms of acceleration and distance:
$$V^2 = 2a s_{\text{acc}} = 2a(50) = 100a$$

Use the deceleration relation $V^2 = 2(2a)s_{\text{dec}}$ to solve for $s_{\text{dec}}$:
$$100a = 4a s_{\text{dec}} \implies s_{\text{dec}} = \frac{100a}{4a} = 25\text{ m}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Link squared velocities:
- Acceleration phase:
$$V^2 = 2a(50) = 100a$$

Solve for braking distance:
- Deceleration rate $2a$:
$$s_{\text{dec}} = \frac{V^2}{2(2a)} = \frac{100a}{4a} = 25\text{ m}$$
The vehicle covers $25\text{ m}$ while braking.

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Practice: Core Practice 1: Train journey between two stations with deceleration twice acceleration

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 1: Train journey between two stations with deceleration twice acceleration

hints: Since deceleration is twice acceleration, the deceleration duration is half the acceleration duration: $t_{\text{dec}} = 0.5T$, giving cruising duration $180 - 1.5T$.
Equate the area of the trapezium to $3300$: $\frac{(180 - 1.5T) + 180}{2} \times 25 = 3300 \implies 360 - 1.5T = 264 \implies 1.5T = 96 \implies T = 64\text{ s}$.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the time durations for each stage in terms of $T$:
$$t_{\text{acc}} = T$$
$$t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{V}{2a} = \frac{aT}{2a} = 0.5T$$
$$t_{\text{cruise}} = 180 - (T + 0.5T) = 180 - 1.5T$$

Express the total distance as the area of the velocity-time trapezium and solve for $T$:
$$s = \frac{t_{\text{cruise}} + T_{\text{total}}}{2} \times V$$
$$3300 = \frac{(180 - 1.5T) + 180}{2} \times 25 = \frac{360 - 1.5T}{2} \times 25$$
$$360 - 1.5T = \frac{3300 \times 2}{25} = 264$$
$$1.5T = 360 - 264 = 96 \implies T = \frac{96}{1.5} = 64\text{ s}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Express stage durations:
- Acceleration and braking times:
$$t_{\text{acc}} = T, \quad t_{\text{dec}} = 0.5T$$
$$t_{\text{cruise}} = 180 - 1.5T$$

Solve for acceleration duration $T$:
- Area of trapezium:
$$\frac{360 - 1.5T}{2} \times 25 = 3300 \implies 1.5T = 96 \implies T = 64\text{ s}$$
The train cruises for $180 - 1.5T$ seconds, and $T = 64\text{ s}$.

ai_rubric.observable: Expresses deceleration time as $0.5T$ and cruising time as $180 - 1.5T$.
Sets up total distance equation using trapezium area: $\frac{(180 - 1.5T) + 180}{2} \times 25 = 3300$.
Solves $12.5(360 - 1.5T) = 3300 \implies 18.75T = 1200$ to obtain $T = 64\text{ s}$.

hints: Acceleration time is $t_{\text{acc}} = \frac{V}{1.25} = 0.8V$, deceleration time is $t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{V}{2.5} = 0.4V$.
Cruising duration is $90 - (0.8V + 0.4V) = 90 - 1.2V$.
Total distance is trapezium area: $\frac{(90 - 1.2V) + 90}{2} \times V = (90 - 0.6V)V = 90V - 0.6V^2 = 1620$.
Rearrange to $0.6V^2 - 90V + 1620 = 0 \implies V^2 - 150V + 2700 = 0$.
Factor $(V - 30)(V - 120) = 0$. For $V = 120$, $t_{\text{acc}} + t_{\text{dec}} = 1.2(120) = 144\text{ s} > 90\text{ s}$, which is impossible. Thus $V = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Express the durations of each of the three stages in terms of $V$:
$$t_{\text{acc}} = \frac{V}{1.25} = 0.8V$$
$$t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{V}{2.5} = 0.4V$$
$$t_{\text{cruise}} = 90 - (0.8V + 0.4V) = 90 - 1.2V$$

Set up the area of the velocity-time trapezium and equate it to $1620\text{ m}$:
$$s = \frac{t_{\text{cruise}} + T_{\text{total}}}{2} \times V$$
$$1620 = \frac{(90 - 1.2V) + 90}{2} \times V = (90 - 0.6V)V = 90V - 0.6V^2$$

Rearrange into standard quadratic form and solve for $V$:
$$0.6V^2 - 90V + 1620 = 0$$
$$V^2 - 150V + 2700 = 0$$
$$(V - 30)(V - 120) = 0$$

Analyze the physical validity of each solution:
$$\text{If } V = 120\text{ m s}^{-1}, \quad t_{\text{acc}} + t_{\text{dec}} = 1.2(120) = 144\text{ s} > 90\text{ s} \quad (\text{impossible})$$
$$\text{Therefore, the unique physical solution is } V = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

$$V^2 - 150V + 2700 = (V - 30)(V - 120) = 0$$

hints: In a non-cruising journey, the velocity-time graph is a single triangle.
Acceleration time is $\frac{V}{1.5} = \frac{2}{3}V$, deceleration time is $\frac{V}{3.0} = \frac{1}{3}V$.
Total time is $T_0 = \frac{2}{3}V + \frac{1}{3}V = V$.
The area of the triangle is $\frac{1}{2} \times T_0 \times V = \frac{1}{2}V^2 = 1200$.
Solve: $V^2 = 2400 \implies V_0 = \sqrt{2400} = 20\sqrt{6} \approx 49.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, so $T_0 \approx 49.0\text{ s}$.

$$T_0 = t_{\text{acc}} + t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{2}{3}V + \frac{1}{3}V = V$$

Set up the area of the triangular velocity-time graph and equate to $1200\text{ m}$:
$$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}(T_0)(V) = \frac{1}{2}V^2$$
$$\frac{1}{2}V^2 = 1200 \implies V^2 = 2400$$
